newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Unhappy rate memories haunt Australian dollar.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Unhappy rate memories haunt Australian dollar.

text.p: The Australian dollar stumbled below 78 cents Tuesday after the market suffered yet another bout of hysterics over domestic interest rates.

The currency had slipped 1/3 cent offshore Monday as U.S. investment banks sold, and looked set to slump through US$0.7770 support this morning as traders swapped loose talk of an imminent easing from the Reserve Bank.

The pressure eased slightly when the RBA kept silent at its 9.30 am slot, the usual window for a rate change, but dealers felt the feverish nature of the speculation boded ill for the currency and looked for a re-test of last week's US$0.7740 low.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local currency had found a fragile foothold at US$0.7778/83 having dipped to US$0.7770 from an early US$0.7784/89 and US$0.7810/15 late here Monday.
A break lower would likely see a re-test of the five-month trough at US$0.7740 and raise the risk of technical tumble to US$0.7680 -- the low point from August last year.
A rally above 78 was needed to counter the immediate bearish pressure and the currency would have to clear US$0.7850/65 to repair the longer term chart outlook.
The jittery mood reflected the market's paranoia since the RBA caught most everyone out with its December 11 rate cut.
Among the more imaginative rumours was that RBA governor Ian Macfarlane had been seen walking into the Sydney headquarters at 5.30 am and such an early start had to mean a rate cut.

Another was that a group of dealers at the RBA had cancelled a golf game today with traders at a Sydney branch of a European bank. As it happened, this rumour actually held a kernel of truth, but the market conclusion that they had to be on board for an easing proved well wide of the mark.
Nevertheless, dealers doubted the market would tire of its sport anytime soon and expected the same sort of tension tomorrow morning -- the last three cuts came on a Wednesday.

Analysts, who are sometimes allowed the luxury of a longer term view, expect the RBA to sit pat until crucial Q4 consumer price data are released on January 29 and then make a final decision on policy at its next board meeting on February 4.
Even then, most only rated the chance of a cut as 50/50, largely on the premise the bank would first want to gauge the impact of the 150 basis points of easing already delivered.

The market had no such reservations and pushed the 90-day bank bill future contract up another four basis points today to 94.35, implying a rate of 5.65 percent compared the present official rate of 6.00 percent.
The risks of a cut might be a little clearer once housing finance and consumer credit are released Wednesday and the politically sensitive jobs data for December are out Thursday.

The latter will be particularly important as the RBA cited the need to reduce unemployment as a major factor behind the last three easings. Thus a weak report would have the market baying for a cut and could see the dollar re-test its lows.
The dollar was not quite as vulnerable on the crosses, however, as sluggish economic growth in Japan and Germany meant rates there would be staying low or even coming down over the next few months.
That outlook helped limit the dollar's losses to 90.55/65 yen and 1.2378/94 marks from 90.70/80 and 1.2383/98 late here Monday.
In trade weighted terms it was off at 58.2 from 58.4.
